title: Send the Envoy, or Overturn the Emperor's Own Decision
actor_role: Acting head of the Council of State (Dajokan) while Chancellor Sanjo Sanetomi was ill; the man with the authority to take the matter back to the Emperor
location: Tokyo, Japan -- the Council of State (Dajokan)
t0: It is mid-to-late October 1873. Two months earlier, on August 17-18, the Council of State and Emperor Meiji formally approved sending Saigo Takamori to Korea as a special envoy -- a proposal Saigo argued for partly on the ground that if Korea killed him, Japan would have unambiguous cause for a punitive expedition. Since then Okubo Toshimichi, Iwakura Tomomi and the rest of the Iwakura Mission have returned from a year and a half touring the industrial and military powers of the United States and Europe, and they want the decision undone. Sanjo Sanetomi, the Chancellor, has fallen ill; Iwakura holds his authority. The Council must either let the approved mission proceed, or reverse a decision the Emperor has already signed.
context_summary: Your government approved sending an envoy to Korea two months ago, with the Emperor's assent. Then your senior colleagues came home from eighteen months in the West and said plainly that Japan cannot afford what this might start. Reversing it means overturning the Emperor's own decision and humiliating the most prominent man in the government.
immediate_outcome: Iwakura, holding acting authority over the Council of State, carried Okubo's case to Emperor Meiji, and the August approval was reversed around October 22-23, 1873. Saigo Takamori resigned as Councillor of State and commander of the Imperial Guard on October 23. Itagaki Taisuke, Goto Shojiro, Eto Shimpei and Soejima Taneomi resigned the following day; the resignations were accepted on October 25. More than a hundred Imperial Guard officers loyal to Saigo also left government service.
long_term_outcome: Japan continued its internal programme -- land tax reform, conscription, industrial development -- and got what it wanted from Korea by narrower means, using the 1875 Ganghwa Island naval incident to force the Treaty of Ganghwa in 1876, without the general war Saigo's proposal risked. The domestic cost arrived separately. Saigo returned to Satsuma and founded private military academies for former samurai; those academies became the organisational and manpower base of the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877, the largest armed uprising the Meiji government ever faced, in which tens of thousands were killed or wounded and Saigo himself died. Eto Shimpei, another of the 1873 resignees, had already led the smaller Saga Rebellion in 1874.
uncertainty_factors: Saigo's actual intent is contested by historians
Qing China's and Russia's likely response unknown
Political cost of reversing an imperial decision

options.label: Let the approved mission proceed and take an assertive posture toward Korea now
options.short_description: Follow through on the Council's August 1873 approval: send Saigo to Korea as special envoy, accepting his own stated reasoning that a rejection or his killing would give Japan clear grounds for a punitive expedition.
options.upside: Acts while the unity and momentum of the Restoration still hold; answers Korea's continued refusal to deal with Japan's new imperial court directly rather than deferring it; gives a large, recently displaced samurai class a national purpose at a moment of real domestic strain; and forecloses the risk that delay lets Korea consolidate its defences or draw closer to Qing China or Russia.
options.downside: Risks military confrontation, possibly general war, before Japan's army, navy and industrial base are remotely comparable to the Western powers -- a gap the returning Mission members had just seen for themselves. It could also pull in Qing China, which had its own long-standing interests in Korea, or complicate matters with Russia.
known_tradeoffs: To officials who had stayed in Japan rather than touring the West, Korea's rebuffs were a live and worsening affront to national standing, and Saigo's willingness to stake his life read as resolve rather than recklessness. versus A war begun before modernisation was far advanced could be ruinously costly, or disastrous if it escaped the bounds of a limited punitive expedition, at a moment when the Meiji state's own institutions were still half-built.

options.label: Reverse the decision and put internal modernisation first
options.short_description: Withdraw the approval for Saigo's mission, defer the Korea question, and turn the government's attention and money toward reform, industry, and building real military and administrative capacity.
options.upside: Avoids committing to a war before the ability to sustain one exists; preserves resources and political capital for land tax reform, conscription and industrial development, which the returning Mission members judged urgent; and avoids provoking a crisis that might draw in Qing China or Russia while Japan is still weak.
options.downside: Overturns a decision the Emperor formally approved only two months earlier -- a grave institutional and personal affront to Saigo and his allies. It risks breaking the political unity of the early Meiji coalition, and it leaves a genuine diplomatic problem unresolved, to be answered later on terms Japan may not control.
known_tradeoffs: Okubo and Iwakura had just spent eighteen months measuring Japan against the industrial and military scale of the West at first hand, and concluded the country could not yet sustain a war however real the grievance. versus The reversal costs the government Saigo and several other senior figures, and removes Saigo's authority over a large body of loyal former-samurai troops.

case_information.content: Korea's Joseon court, under the regency of the Daewongun, had repeatedly refused to accept Japanese diplomatic communications that used the new Meiji-era imperial terminology, and Korean officials had reportedly used insulting language toward Japan in notices posted at Busan.

In a Council of State meeting, Saigo Takamori proposed travelling to Korea himself as special envoy. Multiple accounts record him stating that if Korea killed him, that would give clear and unambiguous justification for a subsequent military expedition. This is his stated reasoning as recorded; what he actually intended is a separate and contested question.
The Council of State and Emperor Meiji had already formally approved sending Saigo as envoy on August 17-18, 1873, before Okubo, Iwakura and the other senior officials returned from abroad.

Okubo Toshimichi argued in a written opinion (his '7 Points Document') that action against Korea was premature because Japan was still early in its own modernisation, and that a war would be far too costly for Japan to sustain at this point.

Okubo, Iwakura, Kido Takayoshi and the other members of the Iwakura Mission had just spent roughly a year and a half touring the industrial and military powers of the United States and Europe, and returned with direct, firsthand impressions of how far behind Japan's own capacity remained.

A large samurai class had recently lost its traditional stipends and social role under Meiji reforms. Some contemporaries -- and some later historians -- held that war with Korea was seen by parts of that class, and by some of Saigo's supporters including Itagaki Taisuke, as an outlet for displaced military energy. This was a belief about motive, not an established fact about it.

Iwakura Tomomi held acting authority over the Council of State in place of the ill Chancellor Sanjo Sanetomi at the time of the final decision, which gave him standing to bring the matter directly before the Emperor.

Saigo, Itagaki, Goto Shojiro, Eto Shimpei and Soejima Taneomi would resign within days of the reversal -- Saigo on October 23, the others on October 24, accepted October 25, 1873 -- along with more than a hundred Imperial Guard officers. That this would follow was not certain to those debating the decision.

Saigo would return to Satsuma and found a network of private military academies for former samurai, which became the organisational base for the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877 -- an armed uprising against the Meiji government in which Saigo died.
Some of the 1873 resignees would lead or inspire earlier armed uprisings, including Eto Shimpei's Saga Rebellion of 1874.

Japan would not mount a major military campaign against Korea in the 1870s. Instead it used a more limited naval incident at Ganghwa Island in 1875 and gunboat diplomacy to force the Treaty of Ganghwa in 1876, opening Korean ports without full-scale war.

Historians remain divided on whether Saigo's envoy proposal genuinely aimed at eventual war. More recent biographical scholarship, notably Mark Ravina's, argues his stated willingness to risk assassination was partly a rhetorical manoeuvre aimed at winning over Itagaki and other domestic rivals, and that his deeper aim may have been closer to establishing a firm direct relationship with Korea than to provoking war. This is an interpretive question, unresolved.

evidence.author_or_institution: Research record for this case (see src-01 through src-07)
evidence.supported_claim: Two points are unsettled and are treated as such. First, Saigo's true intent: the traditional account has him deliberately courting assassination to manufacture a pretext, while Ravina argues this partly reflects his rhetorical positioning in the debate; his stated willingness to risk death is documented, his deeper motive is not. Second, sources broadly agree on approval around August 17-18 and reversal around October 22-23, 1873 but vary in exact-day precision, and they differ on how much of the samurai class's support for the expedition was about finding a new social role versus genuine grievance -- treated here as belief and inference, not settled fact. Note also that several sources in this record are discovery-grade reference pages, used for orientation and cross-checking rather than as authorities.
